title: How much American silver reached China between 1550 and 1800?
short: Estimates of the share of Spanish American silver that ended up in China vary widely because mint, shipping and Chinese monetary records have never been reconciled in one account.

needs.ask: Build a decade-by-decade mass balance for 1550 to 1800 that reconciles registered production, contraband estimates and route flows, and test it against Chinese silver-copper exchange rates and prices.
Read the Manila treasury accounts and galleon registers in the AGI against the Ramo Filipinas in the AGN to produce a reconciled Acapulco-Manila series for 1571 to 1815.
Convert every published figure to tonnes of fine silver with documented assumptions, then propagate the uncertainty to show where mint, treasury and shipping series double count.

matters: The volume of silver entering China is central to the argument that world trade became global after the founding of Manila in 1571, to explanations of the Ming fiscal shift to silver, and to debates over whether a contraction of silver imports helped bring down the Ming in the 1630s–40s. It also bears on European price history, on the Dutch and English East India Companies' balance of trade, and on nineteenth-century arguments that the reversal of silver flows destabilised the Qing.
stuck: Silver reached China by several routes (the Manila galleons, the Cape route via European companies, overland through Central Asia, and from Japan, which was a larger supplier than the Americas for parts of the period), and each route is documented in different archives with different biases. Registered mint and treasury output understates production because of contraband and unregistered silver, and smuggling on the Acapulco–Manila route was extensive. Chinese sources record taxes, prices and exchange rates rather than imports, so arrivals must be inferred, and published estimates (Barrett, Flynn and Giráldez, von Glahn, TePaske) rest on different assumptions about leakage, re-export and Japanese supply.
solved: A route-by-route, decade-by-decade mass balance for 1550–1800 in which American registered production plus an explicit contraband estimate equals the sum of silver retained in the Americas, shipped to Europe, re-exported to Asia, and carried across the Pacific, with China's share derived from these flows and checked against Japanese exports and Chinese monetary indicators (silver–copper exchange rates, tax receipts in silver, price levels).
approach: The registered production series of Garner (1988) and TePaske (2010), the global accounting of Barrett (1990) and the import estimates of Atwell (1982), Flynn and Giráldez (1995) and von Glahn (1996) are the base. Kobata (1965) fixed the scale of Japanese supply, and the galleon histories of Bonialian (2014) and Giráldez (2015) document how much of the Pacific trade escaped registration.

Assemble every published figure into one linked dataset, recording route, decade, original unit (pesos, marks or taels), fineness and whether the number is registered or estimated. Converting all of it to tonnes of fine silver with documented assumptions is what makes the routes comparable and exposes double counting where the same silver appears in mint, treasury and shipping series.

For the Pacific route, read the Manila treasury accounts and galleon registers in the AGI, located through Heredia Herrera (1989), against the Ramo Filipinas in the AGN described by Urrutia de Stebelski (1980). A reconciled Acapulco–Manila series for 1571–1815, set beside contemporary complaints about smuggling, would be useful on its own.

Rival readings of the seventeenth century can then be tested directly. Atwell's case for a collapse of imports after the 1630s and von Glahn's reply in the Journal of Economic History predict different decade totals, while Deng (2008) and Flynn and Giráldez (2002) disagree on how large the inflow was relative to the Chinese economy; VOC finding aids for Deshima and the Canton factory records of the East India Company give independent checks on the Japanese and Cape routes.

On the Chinese side, silver–copper exchange rates and provincial prices from the Qing archives, and from 1736 the Qing Grain Price Database, offer a test of timing rather than volume. Palma and Silva (2024), Irigoin (2009) and Lin (2006) frame the eighteenth-century and closing years, but contraband and the overland route through Central Asia mean China's share will remain a range under stated assumptions.

Progress depends on wider imaging of AGI and AGN legajos, on access to Qing memorials through the First Historical Archives, and on economic historians who read Spanish, Dutch and classical Chinese reviewing each series before it enters the totals.

existing.title: The Production and Uses of Gold and Silver in Sixteenth- and Seventeenth-Century Japan
existing.note: Established the scale of Japanese silver exports, which competed with American silver as a source of China's supply.

existing.title: Guía del ramo Filipinas
existing.venue: México: Archivo General de la Nación (Serie Guías y Catálogos 5)
existing.note: Guide to the 63 volumes of the AGN's Ramo Filipinas, the Mexican side of the Manila galleon administration.

existing.title: International Bullion Flows and the Chinese Economy circa 1530–1650
existing.note: Argued that Japanese and American silver transformed the late Ming economy and that a fall in imports after the 1630s contributed to the dynasty's collapse.

existing.title: Long-Term Silver Mining Trends in Spanish America: A Comparative Analysis of Peru and Mexico
existing.note: Long-run production series for Peruvian and Mexican silver from registered taxes, the base for most later flow estimates.

existing.title: Filipinas en el Archivo General de Indias
existing.venue: In El Extremo Oriente Ibérico: Investigaciones históricas, metodología y estado de la cuestión, Madrid: Agencia Española de Cooperación Internacional and CSIC, 149–183 (revised from Anuario de Estudios Americanos 37, 1980)
existing.note: Classification of the AGI's Audiencia de Filipinas fonds by series, with legajo ranges for the Manila treasury accounts and galleon registers.

existing.title: World Bullion Flows, 1450–1800
existing.venue: In James D. Tracy (ed.), The Rise of Merchant Empires, Cambridge University Press, 224–254
existing.note: First global accounting of bullion production and movement, estimating the shares of American silver that flowed to Europe and on to Asia.

existing.authors: Dennis O. Flynn and Arturo Giráldez
existing.title: Born with a 'Silver Spoon': The Origin of World Trade in 1571
existing.note: Argued that Chinese demand, driven by silver's high value in China, created a global market linked through Manila from 1571 (link is the 2022 reprint).

existing.title: Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000–1700
existing.note: Monetary history of China that produced revised estimates of silver imports by source and period.

existing.title: Myth and Reality of China's Seventeenth-Century Monetary Crisis
existing.note: Challenged Atwell's thesis, arguing that silver imports did not collapse in the 1630s–40s on the scale required to explain the Ming fall.

existing.authors: Dennis O. Flynn and Arturo Giráldez
existing.title: Cycles of Silver: Global Economic Unity through the Mid-Eighteenth Century
existing.note: Extended the argument into a two-cycle model of silver production and Chinese demand through the eighteenth century.

existing.title: China Upside Down: Currency, Society, and Ideologies, 1808–1856
existing.venue: Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Asia Center (Harvard East Asian Monographs 270)
existing.note: Linked the end of the Spanish American silver supply during the independence wars to silver outflow and crisis in Qing China, framing the end point of the period.

existing.title: Miracle or Mirage? Foreign Silver, China's Economy and Globalization from the Sixteenth to the Nineteenth Centuries
existing.note: Argued that foreign silver was small relative to the Chinese economy and questioned claims for its transformative effect.

existing.title: The End of a Silver Era: The Consequences of the Breakdown of the Spanish Peso Standard in China and the United States, 1780s–1850s
existing.note: Showed how Chinese demand for the Spanish peso as a unit, not only as bullion, shaped late flows and their reversal.

existing.authors: John J. TePaske (ed. Kendall W. Brown)
existing.title: A New World of Gold and Silver
existing.note: Posthumous compilation of decade-by-decade registered gold and silver output from Spanish and Portuguese American treasuries and mints, with discussion of contraband.

existing.title: China en la América colonial: Bienes, mercados, comercio y cultura del consumo desde México hasta Buenos Aires
existing.venue: México: Instituto Mora; Buenos Aires: Biblos
existing.note: Traced Asian goods and the silver paid for them through New Spain, Peru and the Río de la Plata, using unpublished Spanish, Mexican, Peruvian and Argentine records, much of it trade outside the registered galleon.

existing.title: The Age of Trade: The Manila Galleons and the Dawn of the Global Economy
existing.note: Full history of the Manila galleon route from 1571 to 1815, with silver as the commodity driving the trade.

existing.title: The Changing Significance of Latin American Silver in the Chinese Economy, 16th–19th Centuries
existing.venue: Revista de Historia Económica / Journal of Iberian and Latin American Economic History (published online 2019)
existing.note: Updated synthesis of import estimates and of silver's changing monetary role in China across three centuries.

existing.authors: Nuno Palma and André C. Silva
existing.title: Spending a Windfall: American Precious Metals and Euro-Asian Trade
existing.note: Quantified how American bullion financed European imports from Asia, a key link in the Cape-route component of flows to China.

archives.repository: Archivo General de Indias, Seville (via PARES)
archives.collection: Contaduría and Filipinas sections: Caja de Manila accounts, galleon registers, Acapulco and Manila customs records
archives.note: Principal source for registered silver on the Acapulco–Manila route; many legajos imaged on PARES, the rest consultable in Seville.

holdings.name: Filipinas: general accounts of the Real Hacienda, 1726-1834
holdings.note: General accounts of the Manila treasury with detailed receipts (cargo) and expenditure (data), described in Heredia Herrera (1989).

holdings.name: Filipinas: testimonies of registros de naos, 1657-1809
holdings.note: Sewn registers formed at the Manila treasury for each galleon, with appraisal of goods, tonnage survey and the allotment of cargo space, sent to Spain; spread over legajos 934-964; series described in Heredia Herrera (1989).

holdings.name: Contaduría, Section II (pre-1726 Philippine accounts)
holdings.note: Heredia Herrera (1989) places the Manila treasury accounts for years before 1726 in the Contaduría rather than in Filipinas.

archives.repository: Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico City
archives.collection: Real Hacienda, Casa de Moneda and Filipinas series
archives.note: Mint and treasury records for New Spain, the main source of Pacific silver; consultation onsite with partial digital access.

holdings.name: Ramo Filipinas
holdings.note: Sixty-three volumes from 1718 on the Philippines and the Manila galleon trade, described in the guide by Urrutia de Stebelski (1980).

holdings.name: Casa de Moneda
holdings.note: Mint records for Mexico City from 1612 to 1856, a principal source for coinage and silver production in New Spain.

archives.repository: Global Price and Income History Group, University of California, Davis
archives.collection: Government budget series, including Klein and TePaske treasury accounts for Mexico, 1576–1816 (hosted on the European State Finance Database)
archives.note: Free downloadable royal treasury series compiled from the Spanish American cajas.

holdings.name: TePaske and Klein royal treasury accounts, Mexico, 1576-1816
holdings.note: Treasury series compiled from the Spanish American cajas; the GPIH file points to the European State Finance Database, and the compiler's papers are at Duke University.

archives.collection: Archives of the Dutch East India Company (VOC), 1602–1795, including bullion shipments and Asian accounts
archives.note: Records of VOC silver exports from Europe and Japanese silver traded through Deshima; much is inventoried and partly imaged.

holdings.name: Archief van de Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie
holdings.note: VOC head-office archive, 1602-1795, including the letters and papers received from Asia.

holdings.name: Nederlandse Factorij in Japan (Hirado and Deshima)
holdings.note: Archive of the Dutch trading post in Japan, 1609-1860, with the Hirado and Deshima daybooks; needed for the Japanese silver and copper trade.

archives.collection: India Office Records: East India Company ledgers, Canton factory records and bullion export accounts
archives.note: Main source for English silver shipments to Canton in the eighteenth century; reading-room access, selected series digitized.

holdings.name: Factory Records: China and Japan
holdings.note: Canton diaries and consultations 1751-1834, China Select Committee secret consultations 1793-1832 and ship diaries 1721-1751.

holdings.name: Records of the East India Company Factory at Canton
holdings.note: Commercial papers on the Company's China trade that partly duplicate G/12 and fill part of the gap 1754-1774.

archives.repository: First Historical Archives of China, Beijing
archives.collection: Qing palace memorials and Board of Revenue records on silver, copper cash exchange rates, grain prices and Guangdong maritime customs
archives.note: Chinese-side evidence for timing and effects of silver inflows; access onsite by application, with some series online.

archives.repository: Institute of Modern History, Academia Sinica, Taipei
archives.collection: Qing Dynasty Grain Price Database (清代糧價資料庫), monthly provincial grain price reports from 1736 to 1911, compiled from the project begun by Wang Yeh-chien
archives.note: Prices reported to the throne in silver taels per picul, drawn from memorials in the National Palace Museum, Taipei, and the First Historical Archives; online after free registration.
